titleText.es: Vale, ahora que la sensación de pérdida le atenaza, pega un frenazo.
titleText.en: Okay, now just as the loss hits him, slam on the brakes.
titleText.noteEn: The title text reveals the final step of the retaliation: after the synthesized voice makes the tailgater feel a sudden personal loss, the driver plans to brake sharply.

regions.labelEs: ESE TIPO ESTÁ MUY PEGADO A MÍ.

applications.explanationEn: Está sets the current position, pegado describes extreme closeness, and a mí supplies the person used as the point of reference; muy only strengthens the degree.
Echaré supplies the future form of echar, while un vistazo completes the conventional quick-look expression.
Echar keeps its full dictionary form and adds -é for a future action by “I.”

regions.labelEs: SU PORTÁTIL ESTÁ ENCENDIDO, PROBABLEMENTE EN EL ASIENTO DE ATRÁS. Y... SÍ, SU WIFI SE AUTOCONECTA.

applications.explanationEn: Probable has the same masculine and feminine form, so adding -mente creates probablemente, the word that marks the location claim as likely rather than certain.

regions.labelEs: AHORA BUSCAMOS ALGÚN EXPLOIT REMOTO... INSTALAMOS UN SINTETIZADOR DE VOZ... Y PROBAMOS CON ALGO PSICOLÓGICO Y OSCURO.

applications.exampleEs: PROBAMOS CON ALGO PSICOLÓGICO Y OSCURO
applications.explanationEn: Probamos changes for “we,” con introduces the chosen approach, and algo psicológico y oscuro fills the complete option being tried.
Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks what. The unaccented connector que has a different job.
Quién carries a written accent because it directly asks who. The plural form is quiénes.

regions.labelEs: SI NO FUERA POR TI, ELLA SEGUIRÍA VIVA.

applications.explanationEn: Si no fuera por forms the fixed counterfactual opening, and ti fills the person whose presence is said to change the outcome.
Si introduces the imagined condition. It has no accent when it means “if.”
Fuera is the -ra form of ser used for the unreal condition; fuese would be an equally valid alternative.
Seguiría is the conditional, or “would,” form that supplies the imagined result.
Seguir keeps its whole dictionary form and adds -ía for a “would” action or state involving one person.
Seguiría gives the hypothetical continuation, and viva is the feminine state that would continue.

cards.noteEn: Ese points to a masculine singular noun that is not presented as right next to the speaker. Feminine singular is esa.

example.en: I do not recognize that sound.

cards.noteEn: In informal speech, tipo can refer to a man as “guy.” In other contexts, it can instead mean a type or kind.

cards.promptEs: estar pegado/pegada a alguien o algo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is stuck to, pressed against, or extremely close to another thing?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of estar, then pegado, pegada, pegados, or pegadas, followed by a and the reference person or thing.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes for the person and time. Pegado changes to match the person or thing being described. A introduces what it is attached or very close to. The expression can describe literal contact or, from context, unusually close proximity.

example.es: La mesa está pegada a la pared.
example.en: The table is right up against the wall.

cards.noteEn: Pegado comes from pegar, “to stick.” With estar and a, it can describe someone or something pressed against or extremely close to another person or thing.

example.es: El armario está pegado a la pared.
example.en: The wardrobe is right up against the wall.

cards.answerEn: to (what someone is tied or attached to)
me (after a preposition such as para)
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses mí after most prepositions. The written accent distinguishes mí (“me”) from mi (“my”).

cards.answerEn: I'll take, as part of echar un vistazo
cards.noteEn: Echar has many meanings, including “to throw” or “to put.” In echar un vistazo, it forms the conventional expression “to take a look.” The ending -é marks a future action by “I.”

example.en: I'll take a look at the report.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone takes a quick look at something?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of echar followed by un vistazo; use a before the thing being viewed when it is stated.
cards.noteEn: Echar has many literal meanings, but echar un vistazo is a conventional expression for looking briefly. Only echar changes for the person and time: echo, echas, echó, echaré. Un vistazo stays together.

example.es: Voy a echar un vistazo al mapa.
example.en: I'm going to take a look at the map.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.
Su agrees with the possessed thing, not with the owner. The same Spanish form can mean his, her, its, their, or formal your; the surrounding context identifies the owner.
As a noun in computing, el portátil is a laptop. As an adjective, portátil means portable.

example.es: Mi portátil necesita una batería nueva.
example.en: My laptop needs a new battery.

cards.noteEn: For a device, encendido means switched on or running. It is the describing form made from encender, “to turn on.”
Probablemente combines probable with -mente to describe a claim as likely rather than certain.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to atrás to describe it as the back or rear one
cards.noteEn: Spanish can put de atrás after an object to identify the one positioned at the back. Natural English usually puts “back” before the noun.
Wifi is used as a Spanish noun. It is often feminine because red, 'network,' is understood: la wifi. Usage and pronunciation vary by region.

example.es: La wifi del hotel es lenta.

cards.answerEn: itself; marks autoconectarse, to connect automatically
cards.noteEn: Autoconectarse uses a matching small word for the thing that connects: me, te, se, nos, or os. Use se with one third-person thing that connects itself or connects automatically.

example.es: El teléfono se autoconecta a la red.
example.en: The phone connects to the network automatically.

cards.noteEn: Autoconecta is a present form used with one device or connection. With se, it describes that thing connecting without the user starting the connection manually.

cards.answerEn: we look for; we search for
cards.noteEn: Buscamos is the present form of buscar for a group that includes the speaker.

example.en: We are looking for a solution.

cards.answerEn: some; some day/time (before a masculine noun)
cards.noteEn: Alguno shortens to algún directly before a masculine singular noun: algún día, algún libro.

example.en: Some neighbor will have the key.

cards.answerEn: security exploit; a way to take advantage of a software flaw
cards.noteEn: Spanish computing language borrows the English noun exploit. It names code or a method that uses a vulnerability to make a system do something unintended.

cards.answerEn: a method that uses a software vulnerability through a network, without physical access to the target device
cards.noteEn: A remote exploit may let an attacker make a vulnerable machine run unintended actions or code from elsewhere. The comic relies on that idea when the nearby laptop is altered through its wireless connection.

cards.answerEn: remote; usable over a network without physical access
cards.noteEn: In computing, remoto describes access or an action performed from another machine or location through a network.
A sintetizador de voz is a speech synthesizer: software or hardware that produces spoken audio.

example.es: El sintetizador produce una voz artificial.
example.en: The synthesizer produces an artificial voice.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”

cards.answerEn: we try; we test an option
cards.noteEn: Probamos is a present form of probar for a group including the speaker. With con, it introduces a person, thing, or approach chosen to see whether it works.

cards.promptEs: probar con + persona, cosa u opción
cards.questionEn: How do you say that you will try a particular person, thing, or option to see whether it works?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of probar, then con, then the person, thing, or option being tried.
cards.noteEn: Probar by itself can mean to try, test, or taste. Con introduces the chosen possibility in this pattern. Only probar changes for the person and time; con stays unchanged.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces the person, thing, or option tried after probar
cards.noteEn: In probar con, con marks the chosen possibility that someone will try to see whether it works. English normally says “try” directly before that option, without a separate word for con.
Oscuro can describe low light literally. Applied to an idea or action, it can instead suggest something disturbing, sinister, or morally grim.

example.es: La historia tiene un final oscuro.
example.en: The story has a dark ending.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.noteEn: Ahí points to a place away from the speaker but normally not as distant as allí. The distinction varies by region and context.

cards.promptEs: si no fuera por alguien o algo
cards.questionEn: How do you say “if it weren't for” a person or thing that changes the outcome?
cards.answerEn: Use si no fuera por, then name the person or thing. Si no fuese por is an equally valid alternative.
cards.noteEn: This expression presents an unreal alternative: without the named factor, the result would be different. Fuera and fuese are two forms of the same hypothetical verb here. The result commonly uses a Spanish “would” form ending in -ría.

example.es: Si no fuera por Ana, llegaríamos tarde.
example.en: If it weren't for Ana, we would arrive late.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe an imagined “if…, …would…” situation?
cards.answerEn: Use si followed by a hypothetical past verb form for the condition, and use a “would” form for the result.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls the condition's verb form the imperfect subjunctive. It often ends in -ra or -se, as in tuviera or tuviese. The result uses the conditional, often ending in -ría, as in haría. In this pattern, do not put the conditional directly after si.

example.en: If I had time, I would travel more.

cards.answerEn: were; were the case, in an unreal condition
cards.noteEn: Fuera is a special form of ser used for a hypothetical situation. In si no fuera por..., it introduces something without which the result would be different. Do not confuse it with fuera meaning “outside.”

example.es: Si fuera fácil, todos lo harían.
example.en: If it were easy, everyone would do it.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes si no fuera por, if it weren't for
cards.noteEn: In the fixed counterfactual expression si no fuera por, por introduces the person or thing whose presence changes the result.

example.es: Si no fuera por Ana, llegaríamos tarde.
example.en: If it weren't for Ana, we would arrive late.

cards.noteEn: Ella is the feminine singular subject pronoun. Spanish often leaves subject pronouns unstated, but ella can be included for clarity or emphasis.
Seguir normally means “to continue.” Before a word describing a condition, it means to remain or still be in that condition. The ending -ía makes this an imagined “would” result.

example.es: Sin ayuda, la puerta seguiría cerrada.
example.en: Without help, the door would still be closed.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of seguir followed by the word that describes the condition.
cards.noteEn: Seguir normally means “to continue” or “to keep going.” Before a description, it means “to still be” or “to remain”: sigue abierta means “is still open.” If the describing word has masculine, feminine, singular, or plural endings, match it to what is being described.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is still in the same condition?

cards.noteEn: Viva is the feminine singular form of vivo and matches one feminine person or thing.

Dios names God, but said by itself it can also react to surprise, excitement, frustration, or strong nostalgia. The tone decides whether natural English keeps ‘God’ or uses an exclamation such as ‘man.’
